about: Infection and Defence (MBBS0014) is the second of the four systems modules in UCL's MBBS Year 1, taught in person in Term 1 (in 2026–27, four weeks in November, before CIF Week A) and carrying 0 credits. UCL's 2026/27 module catalogue says it introduces infectious agents and how they cause disease, the body's defences against them, the epidemiology of infection, its social and psychological consequences for patients, and how anti-infective drugs work. UCL does not publish a topic list, so the topics here follow the order of that official description. Year 1 knowledge is tested in the end-of-year integrated Applied Knowledge Tests.
topics: Bacteria: structure, identification and how they cause disease
Adaptive immunity: T cells, B cells and antibodies
Immune memory, vaccination and when defences fail
Epidemiology, transmission and control of infection
Social and psychological effects of infection on patients
How antimicrobial drugs act, resistance and stewardship

notes.h: Bacteria: structure, identification and how they cause disease
notes.body:
Infection and Defence starts with the organisms themselves. Bacteria are prokaryotes: single cells with no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. Their structure explains how we identify them, how they cause disease and how antibiotics can hit them without harming us.

Key structures
- Chromosome: a single circular DNA molecule in the cytoplasm, often with extra small DNA circles called plasmids. Plasmids frequently carry toxin or antibiotic-resistance genes and can pass between bacteria.
- Ribosomes: 70S (made of 50S and 30S subunits), unlike our 80S ribosomes. This difference is a target for several antibiotics.
- Cell wall: made of peptidoglycan (sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides). Human cells have no peptidoglycan. Mycoplasma has no cell wall at all.
- Outer membrane (Gram-negative bacteria only): contains lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
- Optional extras: a capsule (usually polysaccharide), flagella for movement, pili or fimbriae for attachment, and in some genera (Bacillus, Clostridium and Clostridioides) heat- and disinfectant-resistant spores.

The Gram stain
- Steps: crystal violet, then iodine, then a decolouriser (alcohol or acetone), then a red counterstain such as safranin.
- Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer that keeps the violet dye, so they look purple.
- Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane; the decolouriser removes the violet dye, so they take up the red counterstain and look pink.
- Shape and arrangement narrow the possibilities. Cocci in clusters suggest staphylococci; cocci in chains suggest streptococci; Gram-negative diplococci suggest Neisseria.
- Simple tests help: staphylococci are catalase-positive and streptococci catalase-negative; Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase-positive.
- Mycobacteria (for example Mycobacterium tuberculosis) have waxy mycolic acids in their walls and stain poorly with Gram's method. They are acid-fast, shown with the Ziehl–Neelsen stain.
- Bacteria are also grouped by oxygen needs: obligate aerobes, obligate anaerobes and facultative anaerobes, which can grow with or without oxygen.

From colonisation to disease
Many bacteria live harmlessly on us as commensals (normal flora) and protect us by competing with pathogens. Colonisation means organisms are present without causing harm; infection means they invade and cause a host response or damage. Opportunists cause disease mainly when defences are weakened.

Steps in pathogenesis
- Entry and adhesion: pili and other adhesins bind host cells, for example in the urinary tract.
- Invasion and spread: enzymes break down tissue; some bacteria survive inside cells.
- Evasion: a capsule resists phagocytosis and complement; S. aureus protein A binds the Fc part of antibodies; some bacteria cleave IgA.
- Damage: by toxins and by the host's own inflammatory response.

Toxins
- Exotoxins are proteins secreted by bacteria, often highly specific. Tetanus toxin blocks release of inhibitory transmitters in the spinal cord, causing spastic paralysis. Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing flaccid paralysis. Cholera toxin locks a G protein in its active state, raising cAMP in gut cells, so chloride and water pour into the gut lumen as watery diarrhoea. Diphtheria toxin stops protein synthesis.
- Superantigens (for example toxic shock syndrome toxin-1) link MHC class II molecules to T-cell receptors outside the normal peptide-binding site, activating very many T cells at once and causing a cytokine storm.
- Endotoxin is the lipid A part of LPS in the Gram-negative outer membrane. It is released when bacteria die or divide and is recognised by Toll-like receptor 4, triggering cytokines that cause fever and, in large amounts, septic shock.

Koch's postulates (late 19th century) set out criteria for linking a microbe to a disease, but they fail for organisms that cannot be grown in culture and for asymptomatic carriers.

Exam tips: link each structure to a consequence (stain, virulence or drug target), and do not confuse exotoxins (secreted proteins) with endotoxin (LPS of Gram-negative bacteria).

The other infectious agents differ from bacteria in ways that matter for diagnosis, immunity and treatment.

Viruses
- Viruses are not cells. Each has a genome of DNA or RNA (never both) inside a protein coat called a capsid. Some also have a lipid envelope taken from a host cell membrane.
- They are obligate intracellular parasites: they can replicate only inside a host cell, using its ribosomes and energy.
- Enveloped viruses (for example influenza, HIV, herpesviruses) are generally more easily damaged by drying, detergents and alcohol than non-enveloped viruses (for example norovirus).

The replication cycle
- Attachment: a viral protein binds a specific host receptor, which explains tissue tropism. HIV's gp120 binds CD4 plus a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4); influenza haemagglutinin binds sialic acid on respiratory cells.
- Entry and uncoating: by membrane fusion or endocytosis.
- Replication of the genome and synthesis of viral proteins. Retroviruses such as HIV use reverse transcriptase to copy their RNA into DNA, which integrase inserts into the host genome.
- Assembly and release: by budding (enveloped viruses) or by bursting the cell (lysis). Influenza neuraminidase cuts sialic acid so new virions can escape.

Disease mechanisms
- Direct killing of infected cells, as in HIV destroying CD4 T cells.
- Immune-mediated damage: much of the illness in many viral infections comes from the host response.
- Latency: herpesviruses persist for life. Herpes simplex hides in sensory ganglia and reactivates as cold sores; varicella-zoster reactivates as shingles.
- Transformation: some viruses contribute to cancer, for example human papillomavirus (cervical and other cancers) and hepatitis B and C (liver cancer).

Antigenic variation in influenza A
- Antigenic drift: gradual point mutations in haemagglutinin and neuraminidase, which is why seasonal vaccines are updated.
- Antigenic shift: reassortment of genome segments between strains (influenza A has a segmented genome), producing a new subtype that can cause a pandemic.

Fungi
- Fungi are eukaryotes. Their cell membranes contain ergosterol rather than cholesterol, and their walls contain chitin and glucans; both are drug targets.
- Yeasts (for example Candida) are single cells; moulds (for example Aspergillus) grow as branching filaments called hyphae.
- Many serious fungal infections are opportunistic, affecting people with weakened immunity: invasive aspergillosis in neutropenia, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in advanced HIV.

Parasites
- Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes. Examples are Plasmodium (malaria), Giardia (diarrhoea) and Toxoplasma.
- Malaria is spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes. The parasite multiplies first in the liver and then in red blood cells. Plasmodium falciparum causes the most severe disease.
- Helminths (worms) are multicellular: roundworms (nematodes), tapeworms (cestodes) and flukes (trematodes). They are too large to be engulfed, and the response to them is dominated by Th2 cells, IgE and eosinophils, so eosinophilia in blood is a clue.
- Ectoparasites such as lice and scabies mites live on the skin.

Prions
- Prions are misfolded forms of a normal host protein (PrP) that convert normal PrP into the misfolded form. They contain no nucleic acid.
- They cause transmissible spongiform encephalopathies such as Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD); variant CJD is linked to eating meat from cattle with BSE.
- Prions resist standard sterilisation, which has implications for surgical instruments.

Exam tips: for any organism, be ready to state what kind of agent it is, how it enters and spreads, how it damages the host, and which immune response deals with it.

Innate immunity acts within minutes to hours, does not need previous exposure and recognises broad patterns rather than specific antigens. It does not improve with repeat exposure in the way adaptive immunity does.

Barriers
- Physical: intact skin, tight junctions in epithelia, mucus and the beating cilia of the airways (the mucociliary escalator), and the flushing of urine and tears.
- Chemical: stomach acid, lysozyme in tears and saliva, and antimicrobial peptides such as defensins.
- Biological: commensal bacteria compete with pathogens. Broad-spectrum antibiotics that disturb gut flora can allow Clostridioides difficile to take over.

Recognising danger
- Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) detect pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), structures shared by many microbes but absent from our cells.
- Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are the best known. TLR4 recognises LPS, TLR5 flagellin, TLR3 double-stranded RNA and TLR9 unmethylated CpG DNA. Other families sense microbes inside the cell (NOD-like and RIG-I-like receptors).
- PRRs also detect damage-associated molecular patterns released by injured cells, which is why sterile injury causes inflammation too.

Cells of innate immunity
- Neutrophils: the most numerous white cells in blood, the first to arrive at a site of acute bacterial infection, short-lived phagocytes and the main cells in pus.
- Monocytes and macrophages: phagocytes that also release cytokines and present antigen.
- Dendritic cells: capture antigen in tissues and carry it to lymph nodes to activate naive T cells, bridging innate and adaptive immunity.
- Natural killer (NK) cells: kill virus-infected and tumour cells that have lost MHC class I ("missing self"), and cells coated with antibody.
- Mast cells, basophils and eosinophils: release mediators; important in allergy and in defence against parasites.

Complement
- A cascade of plasma proteins, activated by three routes: classical (antibody bound to antigen, via C1q), lectin (mannose-binding lectin on microbial sugars) and alternative (spontaneous activation on microbial surfaces).
- All routes converge on C3 convertase, which splits C3.
- C3b coats microbes (opsonisation) so phagocytes engulf them more easily.
- C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins that increase vascular permeability; C5a is a strong attractant for neutrophils.
- C5b to C9 form the membrane attack complex, which punches holes in some bacteria. People lacking terminal components are prone to recurrent Neisseria infections.

Phagocytosis and killing
- Opsonins (IgG and C3b) bind receptors on phagocytes. The engulfed microbe sits in a phagosome, which fuses with lysosomes.
- The NADPH oxidase produces reactive oxygen species (the respiratory burst). Its absence causes chronic granulomatous disease, with recurrent bacterial and fungal infections.

Acute inflammation
- Classic signs: redness, heat, swelling and pain (described by Celsus), with loss of function added later.
- Vascular changes: arteriolar dilation raises blood flow (redness, heat); venules become leaky, letting protein-rich fluid (exudate) into tissue (swelling).
- Neutrophil recruitment: cells slow and roll along activated endothelium (selectins), stick firmly (integrins binding ICAM-1), squeeze between endothelial cells (transmigration) and move up chemical gradients (chemotaxis, for example towards IL-8 and C5a).
- Cytokines IL-1, TNF-α and IL-6 act on the hypothalamus to raise the temperature set point (fever) and, mainly through IL-6, make the liver release acute phase proteins such as C-reactive protein (CRP).
- Type I interferons from virus-infected cells put neighbouring cells into an antiviral state.

When the response becomes harmful
Sepsis is defined (Sepsis-3, 2016) as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. It shows that the host response, not only the microbe, causes damage.

Exam tips: be able to sequence leucocyte recruitment step by step and name the molecule at each step; questions often test which complement products do what.

notes.h: Adaptive immunity: T cells, B cells and antibodies
notes.body:
Adaptive immunity is specific (each lymphocyte recognises one antigen) and has memory, so a second encounter brings a faster and stronger response. It takes days to develop on first exposure.

Where lymphocytes come from
- All lymphocytes arise in the bone marrow. B cells mature there; T cells mature in the thymus.
- In the thymus, positive selection keeps T cells whose receptors can recognise self-MHC; negative selection removes those that bind self-antigens too strongly. This creates central tolerance. Regulatory T cells add peripheral tolerance.

Antigen presentation and MHC
- T cells do not recognise free antigen. They recognise short peptides presented on major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules, called HLA in humans (genes on chromosome 6).
- MHC class I is on almost all nucleated cells. It shows peptides from inside the cell (for example viral proteins) to CD8 T cells.
- MHC class II is on professional antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells). It shows peptides from material taken up from outside to CD4 T cells.
- A memory aid: CD8 × class I = 8, and CD4 × class II = 8.

Activating a naive T cell
- Signal 1: the T-cell receptor binds the peptide–MHC complex.
- Signal 2: co-stimulation, mainly CD28 on the T cell binding CD80/CD86 (B7) on the dendritic cell. Signal 1 without signal 2 tends to cause anergy (unresponsiveness).
- Signal 3: cytokines steer which kind of helper cell develops.
- The activated cell divides rapidly (clonal expansion) and differentiates into effector and memory cells.

CD4 helper T-cell subsets
- Th1: produce IFN-γ, activate macrophages; key against intracellular pathogens such as mycobacteria.
- Th2: produce IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13; drive IgE and eosinophils against helminths; also involved in allergy.
- Th17: produce IL-17, recruit neutrophils; important against extracellular bacteria and fungi.
- T follicular helper cells: help B cells in germinal centres.
- Regulatory T cells (FOXP3-positive): suppress responses and maintain tolerance.

CD8 cytotoxic T cells
They recognise infected or abnormal cells through MHC class I and kill them by releasing perforin and granzymes, or through Fas–Fas ligand, triggering apoptosis.

B cells and antibodies
- Each B cell carries a B-cell receptor, a membrane-bound antibody. Most protein antigens need T-cell help (T-dependent responses).
- In germinal centres of lymph nodes, B cells undergo class switching (needs CD40 on the B cell binding CD40 ligand on the helper T cell) and somatic hypermutation with selection, which increases affinity (affinity maturation).
- They become plasma cells, which secrete antibody, or long-lived memory B cells.

Antibody structure: two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains. The Fab region binds antigen; the Fc region determines what the antibody does (binding to Fc receptors and complement).

Antibody classes
- IgM: first antibody made in a primary response; a pentamer, very good at activating complement.
- IgG: the most abundant antibody in serum; four subclasses; crosses the placenta; opsonises and activates complement.
- IgA: a dimer in secretions (gut, airways, breast milk), protecting mucosal surfaces.
- IgE: binds mast cells and basophils; involved in allergy and anti-helminth defence.
- IgD: found mainly on naive B cells as a receptor.

Antibody functions: neutralisation (blocking toxins or viral attachment), opsonisation, complement activation, and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity by NK cells.

Primary and secondary responses
- Primary: a lag of about a week or more, mostly IgM at first, lower affinity.
- Secondary: faster, larger, mainly IgG (or IgA, IgE) of higher affinity, because memory cells are already present. This is the basis of vaccination.

Exam tips: tie each cell type to its MHC class, its cytokines and the type of pathogen it controls; questions often ask which antibody class fits a scenario.

notes.h: Immune memory, vaccination and when defences fail
notes.body:
Vaccination uses immune memory deliberately. Failures of the immune system, whether too weak or misdirected, explain many clinical patterns.

Types of immunity
- Active immunity: your own immune system responds, after infection (natural) or vaccination (artificial). It takes time but gives memory.
- Passive immunity: ready-made antibody is transferred, giving immediate but short-lived protection with no memory. Natural examples are maternal IgG crossing the placenta and IgA in breast milk; artificial examples are immunoglobulin products.

Types of vaccine
- Live attenuated (weakened) organisms, for example MMR, BCG, rotavirus and the nasal influenza vaccine for children. They give strong, long-lasting responses, including T-cell responses, but are generally avoided in significant immunosuppression and in pregnancy.
- Inactivated (killed) whole organisms, for example inactivated polio vaccine.
- Toxoids: inactivated toxins, for example tetanus and diphtheria.
- Subunit or recombinant proteins, for example hepatitis B surface antigen, and HPV virus-like particles.
- Conjugate vaccines: bacterial capsule polysaccharide joined to a carrier protein (for example Hib, meningococcal and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines). Plain polysaccharides trigger a T-independent response that is weak in children under about two and gives little memory. Linking them to protein recruits helper T cells, so infants respond and memory forms.
- mRNA and viral-vector vaccines, used widely against COVID-19, deliver genetic instructions so the body makes the antigen.
- Adjuvants (for example aluminium salts) boost the innate signals that help start a response.

In the UK the reference for vaccines, schedules and contraindications is UKHSA's Green Book (Immunisation against infectious disease). The routine schedule changes from time to time, so always check the current version rather than memorising an old one.

Immunodeficiency
- Primary (inherited) immunodeficiencies are rare. Examples: X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (BTK mutation, no mature B cells), where bacterial infections start once maternal IgG wanes in the second half of the first year; DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion), where a small or absent thymus reduces T cells; severe combined immunodeficiency; chronic granulomatous disease; and complement deficiencies.
- Secondary immunodeficiencies are far more common: HIV infection, chemotherapy and other immunosuppressive drugs, malnutrition, diabetes, and loss of the spleen.
- The pattern of infection points to the defect: antibody or complement problems give recurrent bacterial infections, especially with encapsulated bacteria; T-cell problems give viral, fungal and intracellular infections; neutrophil problems give bacterial and fungal infections.
- After splenectomy, people are at risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b, meningococcus).

HIV and AIDS
HIV infects CD4 T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells. Untreated, the CD4 count falls over years. AIDS is diagnosed when the count falls below about 200 cells per microlitre or an AIDS-defining illness appears (for example Pneumocystis pneumonia). Effective combination antiretroviral therapy suppresses the virus and allows CD4 recovery.

Hypersensitivity (Gell and Coombs, 1963)
- Type I (immediate, IgE-mediated): allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells, releasing histamine within minutes. Examples: hay fever, allergic asthma, anaphylaxis.
- Type II (antibody against cell or tissue antigens): for example haemolytic transfusion reactions and Goodpasture's disease.
- Type III (immune complexes deposited in tissues): for example serum sickness, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and SLE.
- Type IV (delayed, T-cell mediated, peaking after one to three days): for example contact dermatitis and the tuberculin skin test.

Exam tips: for vaccine questions, link the vaccine type to the kind of response it produces; for immunodeficiency, work from the pattern of infections back to the component that is missing.

notes.h: Epidemiology, transmission and control of infection
notes.body:
The epidemiology of infection asks who gets infected, how it spreads and how spread can be stopped.

The chain of infection
Agent, reservoir (where it lives: people, animals, environment), portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Infection control breaks one or more links.

Modes of transmission
- Contact: direct (touch, sexual contact) or indirect via contaminated objects (fomites) and hands.
- Respiratory: traditionally split into large droplets that fall within a short distance and small airborne particles (aerosols) that stay suspended and travel further, such as measles and tuberculosis. Since COVID-19 many experts see this as a spectrum of particle sizes rather than two separate routes; how much each contributes for a given infection is still debated.
- Faecal–oral: contaminated food, water or hands (for example norovirus, hepatitis A).
- Vector-borne: insects such as mosquitoes (malaria).
- Blood-borne: needles, transfusion (for example hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV).
- Vertical: mother to baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding.

Key terms
- Incubation period: from infection to the first symptoms.
- Infectious period: when a person can transmit; it can begin before symptoms.
- Carrier: an infected person who transmits but has no symptoms.
- Endemic: constantly present in a population. Epidemic: more cases than expected. Pandemic: an epidemic across several countries or continents. Outbreak: two or more linked cases, or more cases than expected in one place.
- Incidence: new cases in a period. Prevalence: all existing cases at a time.
- Case fatality ratio: deaths among people with the disease divided by the number of cases.

Reproduction numbers and herd immunity
- The basic reproduction number R0 is the average number of secondary cases from one case in a fully susceptible population. It depends on the organism, contact patterns and setting, so published values are ranges, not constants.
- The effective reproduction number R is roughly R0 × the proportion still susceptible (in the simplest model). An epidemic grows while R > 1 and declines when R < 1.
- Herd immunity threshold: H = 1 − 1/R0. Worked example: if R0 = 10, H = 1 − 1/10 = 0.9, so about 90% must be immune.
- Because no vaccine is 100% effective, the coverage needed is H ÷ vaccine effectiveness. With R0 = 10 and a vaccine 95% effective: 0.9 ÷ 0.95 ≈ 0.947, so about 95% coverage.
- Measles has a very high R0 (often quoted as roughly 12 to 18), giving a threshold of roughly 92% to 94%, which is why very high vaccine coverage is needed.

Surveillance and notification (England)
- Under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010, a registered medical practitioner must notify the proper officer of the local authority on suspicion of a notifiable disease, without waiting for laboratory confirmation. In practice this goes to the local UKHSA health protection team.
- Written notice is due within 3 days; urgent cases should also be reported by phone as soon as reasonably practicable.
- Diagnostic laboratories separately notify UKHSA of specified causative agents.

Outbreak investigation
- Confirm the outbreak and the diagnosis, write a case definition, find cases and plot an epidemic curve. A single sharp peak suggests a point source (for example one contaminated meal); successive waves suggest person-to-person (propagated) spread.
- Control: remove the source, isolate cases, trace and advise contacts, offer vaccination or post-exposure prophylaxis where appropriate.

Healthcare-associated infection
- Standard infection control precautions apply to every patient: hand hygiene, personal protective equipment, safe sharps handling and a clean environment. Transmission-based precautions are added for specific infections.
- The WHO's five moments for hand hygiene: before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching the patient's surroundings.
- Alcohol hand rub does not kill Clostridioides difficile spores and is less reliable against norovirus, so soap and water are used for these.

Exam tips: show your working for R and herd immunity calculations, and remember that the threshold is about immunity, while the coverage target also depends on vaccine effectiveness.

notes.h: Social and psychological effects of infection on patients
notes.body:
UCL's description of Infection and Defence includes the social and psychological consequences of infection. Infection is not only a biological event: it can change how people see themselves, how others treat them, and whether they seek and stick with care.

Stigma
- The sociologist Erving Goffman (Stigma, 1963) described stigma as an attribute that discredits a person and reduces them, in others' eyes, from a whole person to a tainted one. Later work (for example Link and Phelan, 2001) stresses that stigma combines labelling, stereotyping, separation, loss of status and discrimination, and depends on power.
- Infections with a long history of stigma include HIV, tuberculosis, hepatitis B and C, sexually transmitted infections and leprosy; outbreaks such as COVID-19 and mpox have been accompanied by blame directed at particular groups.
- Effects: delay in testing and seeking care, reluctance to tell partners or family, poorer adherence to treatment, loss of work or relationships, and shame or depression.
- Counter-messages matter. For HIV, large studies (PARTNER and others) found no sexual transmission from people whose virus was suppressed to undetectable levels on treatment, summed up as "Undetectable = Untransmittable" (U=U).

Psychological effects
- Anxiety and fear about the illness, about infecting others and about the future.
- Depression, especially with chronic infections, disfigurement or long illness.
- Isolation for infection control can be lonely and frightening. Reviews of mainly observational studies have linked contact isolation in hospital with more anxiety and depression and, in some studies, less contact with clinicians, so isolated patients need extra attention.
- Severe infection can cause delirium, especially in older people, and survivors of critical illness such as sepsis may have lasting psychological problems, including post-traumatic stress symptoms.
- Some people have persistent symptoms after infection (for example after COVID-19). The causes and best management of these conditions are still being researched and remain debated, so take symptoms seriously without overstating what is known.

The sick role
Talcott Parsons (The Social System, 1951) described the sick role: the sick person is excused normal duties and not blamed for being ill, but is expected to want to get better and to seek and cooperate with medical help. Critics note that it fits acute illness better than chronic illness and that stigmatised illnesses are often blamed on the patient.

Social determinants of infection
- Poverty, overcrowding, homelessness, imprisonment and poor-quality housing raise the risk of infections such as tuberculosis.
- Migration from countries with high rates of some infections, barriers to registering with a GP and fear of charges or immigration checks can delay diagnosis.
- Occupation matters: healthcare workers, people who work with animals and sex workers face particular risks.
- Infection can push people into hardship: lost earnings during illness or isolation, and caring responsibilities for others.

Public health versus the individual
- Some measures restrict individuals for the good of others: isolation, exclusion from work or school, contact tracing and partner notification. These raise ethical questions about liberty, confidentiality and fairness, and they work better with explanation and practical support.
- Statutory notification is a legal duty. Beyond that, GMC guidance allows disclosure of confidential information without consent only in limited circumstances, such as when it is in the public interest to protect others from serious harm.

Vaccine hesitancy
A WHO advisory group's model describes three Cs: confidence (trust in vaccines and the system), complacency (low perceived risk) and convenience (access). Listening to concerns and giving clear, honest information works better than dismissing people.

Exam tips: in communication or ethics questions about infection, acknowledge the patient's feelings, explain transmission and treatment clearly, address stigma, and balance confidentiality against the protection of others.

notes.h: How antimicrobial drugs act, resistance and stewardship
notes.body:
This topic covers how anti-infective drugs work in principle. It does not cover prescribing or doses, which are always taken from current local guidelines and the BNF.

Selective toxicity
A good antimicrobial hits a target that the microbe has and we lack, or that differs enough to be hit selectively.

Main antibacterial targets (classic examples)
- Cell wall synthesis. β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) bind penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) and stop peptidoglycan cross-linking. Glycopeptides such as vancomycin bind the D-alanyl-D-alanine end of wall precursors; they are too large to cross the Gram-negative outer membrane, so they act on Gram-positive bacteria.
- Protein synthesis on 70S ribosomes. Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines act on the 30S subunit; macrolides act on the 50S subunit. Aminoglycosides need oxygen-dependent uptake, so they do not work against anaerobes.
- Nucleic acid synthesis. Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; rifampicin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase; metronidazole is activated inside anaerobic organisms and damages their DNA.
- Folate synthesis. Bacteria must make their own folate; sulfonamides block dihydropteroate synthase and trimethoprim blocks dihydrofolate reductase.
- Cell membrane. Polymyxins (for example colistin) bind lipopolysaccharide and disrupt the outer and inner (cytoplasmic) membranes of Gram-negative bacteria.

Useful concepts
- Bactericidal drugs kill bacteria; bacteriostatic drugs stop growth and rely on host defences to clear the organism. The distinction depends on organism and concentration, and matters most where host defences are weak (for example endocarditis, meningitis, neutropenia).
- Spectrum: narrow-spectrum drugs hit few organisms; broad-spectrum drugs hit many but disturb normal flora more, raising the risk of C. difficile and of selecting resistance.
- Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC): the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth in the laboratory.
- Killing pattern: β-lactams depend mainly on time above the MIC, whereas aminoglycosides depend mainly on peak concentration.

Antivirals and antifungals
- Antivirals target steps unique to the virus. Aciclovir is activated by herpesvirus thymidine kinase, so it mainly affects infected cells, then stops viral DNA synthesis. Neuraminidase inhibitors (for example oseltamivir) stop influenza release. HIV is treated with combinations acting on reverse transcriptase, protease and integrase, which makes resistance much less likely.
- Antifungals exploit fungal differences: azoles block ergosterol synthesis; polyenes (amphotericin, nystatin) bind ergosterol and make pores; echinocandins block β-glucan synthesis in the wall.

Resistance
- Intrinsic resistance is natural, such as the outer membrane keeping vancomycin out of Gram-negatives. Acquired resistance arises by mutation or by gaining genes from other bacteria.
- Gene transfer: conjugation (plasmids passed through a pilus), transformation (uptake of free DNA) and transduction (carried by bacteriophages).
- Mechanisms: enzymes that destroy the drug (β-lactamases, including extended-spectrum β-lactamases and carbapenemases); altered targets (MRSA's mecA gene encodes PBP2a, which β-lactams bind poorly; vancomycin-resistant enterococci change D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac); reduced entry (loss of porins); and efflux pumps.
- Every use of an antimicrobial selects for resistant organisms, so unnecessary use matters.

Stewardship in the UK (checked October 2026)
- NICE guideline NG15 (2015) sets out systems and processes for antimicrobial stewardship.
- UKHSA's Start smart then focus toolkit (updated 2023): start only when there is evidence of infection, take cultures first where possible without delaying treatment of sepsis, and document indication, duration or review date. Review at 48 to 72 hours and decide to cease, amend, refer (for example to outpatient therapy), extend with a stop date, or switch from intravenous to oral.
- The UK's national action plan Confronting antimicrobial resistance 2024 to 2029 aims, among other targets, to cut total antibiotic use in humans by 5% from the 2019 to 2020 baseline by 2029, and for 70% of antibiotic use to come from the "Access" category of the UK-adapted version of the WHO AWaRe classification (UK-AWaRe).

Exam tips: for any drug class, state the target, why it is selective, and one mechanism of resistance; never quote doses in this module.

cards.f: Why do Gram-positive bacteria stain purple?
cards.b: Their thick peptidoglycan wall keeps the crystal violet–iodine complex after decolourising; Gram-negatives (thin peptidoglycan plus outer membrane) lose it and take up the red counterstain.
Bacteria have 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S subunits); human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S. The difference allows selective antibiotic targeting.
Exotoxins are proteins secreted by Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria, often very specific. Endotoxin is lipid A of LPS in the Gram-negative outer membrane, recognised by TLR4.
Distinguishes staphylococci (catalase-positive) from streptococci (catalase-negative), both Gram-positive cocci.
Bacteria with mycolic acid-rich walls (e.g. Mycobacterium tuberculosis) that resist acid–alcohol decolourising; shown with the Ziehl–Neelsen stain.
A toxin (e.g. TSST-1) that links MHC class II to T-cell receptors outside the peptide groove, activating very many T cells and causing massive cytokine release.
Colonisation: organisms present and multiplying without harm or host response. Infection: invasion causing tissue damage or a host response.
Usually polysaccharide; helps bacteria resist phagocytosis and complement, so it is an important virulence factor (e.g. pneumococcus, meningococcus).

cards.f: Why are viruses obligate intracellular parasites?
cards.b: They lack ribosomes and their own metabolism, so they can only make proteins and copy their genomes inside a host cell.
Drift: gradual point mutations in haemagglutinin/neuraminidase (seasonal epidemics). Shift: reassortment of genome segments creating a new subtype (pandemic risk).
gp120 binds CD4, plus a co-receptor: CCR5 or CXCR4.
Sensory nerve ganglia; the virus reactivates to cause recurrent lesions such as cold sores.
Ergosterol (humans use cholesterol); it is the target of azole and polyene antifungals.

cards.f: Immune response typical of helminth infection
cards.b: Th2-dominated: IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13, IgE production and eosinophils; blood eosinophilia is a clue.
A misfolded form of host prion protein (PrP) with no nucleic acid that converts normal PrP; causes CJD; resists standard sterilisation.
Pathogen-associated molecular pattern: a structure shared by many microbes but absent from host cells (e.g. LPS, flagellin), recognised by pattern recognition receptors.
Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), working with CD14 and MD-2.
Classical (antibody–antigen complexes via C1q), lectin (mannose-binding lectin) and alternative (spontaneous C3 activation on microbial surfaces).

cards.f: Functions of C3b, C5a and C5b–C9
cards.b: C3b: opsonin. C5a (and C3a): anaphylatoxin, increases permeability; C5a attracts neutrophils. C5b–C9: membrane attack complex.
Margination, rolling (selectins), firm adhesion (integrins binding ICAM-1), transmigration between endothelial cells, then chemotaxis (e.g. IL-8, C5a).
Defect in phagocyte NADPH oxidase, so no respiratory burst; recurrent bacterial and fungal infections.

cards.f: Which cytokine mainly drives CRP production?
cards.b: IL-6, acting on the liver (IL-1 and TNF-α also contribute to the acute phase response).
Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.

cards.f: MHC class I vs class II
cards.b: Class I: almost all nucleated cells, presents intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells. Class II: professional APCs, presents peptides from external material to CD4 T cells.
Co-stimulation, mainly CD28 on the T cell binding CD80/CD86 (B7) on the antigen-presenting cell; without it the T cell tends to become anergic.

cards.f: Th1 vs Th2 vs Th17 cytokines
cards.b: Th1: IFN-γ (macrophage activation). Th2: IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 (IgE, eosinophils). Th17: IL-17 (neutrophil recruitment).
IgG.

cards.f: First antibody class in a primary response
cards.b: IgM, a pentamer that activates complement well.

cards.f: Main antibody in mucosal secretions and breast milk
cards.b: IgA, secreted as a dimer.
Helper T-cell contact via CD40 ligand binding CD40 on the B cell, plus cytokines; it occurs mainly in germinal centres.
By releasing perforin and granzymes, or via Fas–Fas ligand, triggering apoptosis of the target cell.
Active: own immune response (infection or vaccine), slower but with memory. Passive: transferred antibody (maternal IgG, immunoglobulin), immediate, short-lived, no memory.

cards.f: Why conjugate vaccines work in infants
cards.b: Joining capsule polysaccharide to a protein recruits helper T cells, turning a weak T-independent response into a T-dependent one with memory.
MMR, BCG, rotavirus, nasal influenza vaccine for children; generally avoided in significant immunosuppression and pregnancy.
Encapsulated bacteria: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b and Neisseria meningitidis.
BTK mutation stops B-cell maturation; boys get recurrent bacterial infections once maternal IgG wanes in the second half of the first year.
I: IgE immediate. II: antibody against cell/tissue antigens. III: immune complexes. IV: delayed T-cell mediated.
UKHSA's Green Book, Immunisation against infectious disease: vaccines, schedules and contraindications (check the current online chapter).
H = 1 − 1/R0 (simple homogeneous model). Coverage needed = H ÷ vaccine effectiveness.
R0: secondary cases per case in a fully susceptible population. Effective R ≈ R0 × proportion susceptible; spread grows if R > 1.
Incidence: new cases over a period. Prevalence: all existing cases at a point or over a period.
Registered medical practitioners notify the local authority proper officer (via UKHSA health protection team) on suspicion, in writing within 3 days; by phone promptly if urgent.
Point source: one sharp peak about one incubation period after exposure. Propagated: successive, rising waves from person-to-person spread.

cards.f: WHO five moments for hand hygiene
cards.b: Before touching a patient; before clean/aseptic procedures; after body fluid exposure risk; after touching a patient; after touching patient surroundings.
Soap and water, because alcohol hand rub does not kill its spores.
Deaths from a disease divided by the number of people with that disease (diagnosed cases), over a stated period.
An attribute that deeply discredits a person, reducing them in others' eyes from a whole person to a tainted, discounted one.
Undetectable = Untransmittable: people with HIV whose viral load is suppressed to undetectable levels on treatment do not transmit HIV sexually.
Rights: excused normal duties and not blamed for illness. Duties: want to get well, seek and cooperate with medical help.
Linked in mainly observational studies with more anxiety and depression and, in some studies, less contact with clinicians.
Poverty, overcrowding, homelessness, imprisonment, migration from high-incidence countries, HIV, drug or alcohol misuse.

cards.f: WHO advisory group 3Cs of vaccine hesitancy
cards.b: Confidence, complacency and convenience.
They bind penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) and block peptidoglycan cross-linking, weakening the cell wall.

cards.f: Why vancomycin does not work on Gram-negative bacteria
cards.b: It is too large to cross the Gram-negative outer membrane to reach its D-Ala-D-Ala target.
The mecA gene encodes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for β-lactams.
The lowest antimicrobial concentration that prevents visible growth of an organism in vitro.

cards.f: Three routes of horizontal gene transfer
cards.b: Conjugation (plasmid via pilus), transformation (uptake of free DNA) and transduction (carried by bacteriophage).

cards.f: Start smart then focus: review timing and outcomes
cards.b: Review at 48–72 hours: cease, amend, refer (e.g. OPAT), extend with a documented stop/review date, or switch IV to oral.
Herpesvirus thymidine kinase activates it, so it accumulates in infected cells, where it stops viral DNA synthesis.

cards.f: UK AMR national action plan 2024–2029 human use targets
cards.b: Cut total human antibiotic use 5% from the 2019–20 baseline by 2029; 70% of use from the Access category (UK-AWaRe classification).

questions.q: A patient develops spastic paralysis after a contaminated wound. The responsible toxin blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters in the spinal cord. Which organism produces it?
questions.why: Tetanus toxin from Clostridium tetani stops inhibitory interneurons releasing their transmitters, so motor neurons fire unchecked and muscles go into spasm. Botulinum toxin is the classic confusion: it also comes from a Clostridium but blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, giving flaccid, not spastic, paralysis. Cholera toxin raises cAMP in gut epithelium and causes watery diarrhoea, not paralysis. Diphtheria toxin inhibits protein synthesis; its effects are local throat damage and toxic damage to heart and nerves, not spasm from wound infection.

questions.q: Which component of a bacterium is endotoxin?
options: Peptidoglycan of the Gram-positive cell wall
A protein toxin secreted by Gram-positive bacteria
Lipid A of lipopolysaccharide in the Gram-negative outer membrane
questions.why: Endotoxin is lipid A, part of the lipopolysaccharide found only in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, and it triggers TLR4. Peptidoglycan is a cell-wall polymer present in both Gram types and is not what 'endotoxin' means, though it is also recognised by innate receptors. A secreted protein toxin is the definition of an exotoxin, the opposite category. The capsule is a virulence factor that resists phagocytosis but is not a toxin.

questions.q: Outline the steps of the Gram stain and explain why Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria end up different colours.
markScheme: Crystal violet applied, then iodine (forms a dye complex)
Decolouriser (alcohol or acetone) applied, then red counterstain (e.g. safranin)
Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan retains the violet complex, so purple
Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan and outer membrane; violet washed out, counterstain taken up, so pink
questions.modelAnswer: The smear is flooded with crystal violet, then iodine, which forms a large dye–iodine complex in the cells. A decolouriser such as alcohol or acetone is then applied, followed by a red counterstain such as safranin. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that traps the violet complex during decolourising, so they stay purple. Gram-negative bacteria have only a thin peptidoglycan layer beneath an outer membrane; the decolouriser disrupts the outer membrane and the violet complex is washed out, so the cells take up the counterstain and appear pink.

questions.q: Why does influenza A, but not most other respiratory viruses, periodically cause pandemics through antigenic shift?
options: It becomes latent in neurons and reactivates years later
It integrates into the host genome using integrase
Its RNA polymerase has no proofreading, so it accumulates point mutations
Its genome is segmented, so two strains infecting one cell can swap whole segments
questions.why: Shift needs reassortment: influenza A's genome is split into segments, so co-infection with two strains can produce a virus with a new haemagglutinin or neuraminidase, a subtype to which few people are immune. Error-prone copying without proofreading is real, but it produces gradual point mutations, which is antigenic drift, not shift. Latency in neurons describes herpesviruses. Integration with integrase describes retroviruses such as HIV.

questions.q: A patient with advanced HIV develops pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii. What kind of organism is this?
questions.why: Pneumocystis jirovecii is classified as a fungus, an opportunist that causes pneumonia when CD4 counts are very low. It was once thought to be a protozoan, which is why that answer is a tempting historical error. It is not a bacterium: it is a eukaryote. It is not a virus: it is a cellular organism.

questions.q: Describe the main stages of a viral replication cycle, using one named virus to illustrate attachment.
markScheme: Attachment of a viral protein to a specific host receptor (named example, e.g. HIV gp120 to CD4 with CCR5/CXCR4, or influenza haemagglutinin to sialic acid)
Entry (fusion or endocytosis) and uncoating of the genome
Replication of the genome and synthesis of viral proteins using host ribosomes
Assembly and release by budding or cell lysis
questions.modelAnswer: A virus first attaches to its target cell: for example, influenza haemagglutinin binds sialic acid on respiratory epithelium, which explains why it infects the airway. The virus then enters by membrane fusion or endocytosis and uncoats, releasing its genome. The genome is copied and viral proteins are made on the host's ribosomes; retroviruses such as HIV first reverse-transcribe their RNA into DNA. New capsids and genomes are assembled, and the virions leave by budding through the cell membrane, which gives them an envelope, or by lysing the cell.

questions.q: A patient has recurrent meningococcal infections. Deficiency of which part of the immune system most likely explains this?
questions.why: Neisseria species are particularly controlled by the membrane attack complex, so deficiency of C5 to C9 classically causes recurrent Neisseria infection. IgE defends against helminths and drives allergy; its absence would not single out meningococci. NADPH oxidase deficiency (chronic granulomatous disease) causes infections with catalase-positive bacteria and fungi such as Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus, not a specific Neisseria problem. Eosinophils are mainly anti-parasite cells.

questions.q: In acute inflammation, which step in neutrophil recruitment depends mainly on selectins?
questions.why: Selectins make weak, rapidly reversible bonds that slow neutrophils so they roll along activated endothelium. Firm adhesion is the next step and needs integrins on the neutrophil binding ICAM-1 on the endothelium, so choosing it mixes up the two adhesion families. Transmigration is the later squeeze between endothelial cells. Killing happens after phagocytosis and depends on the respiratory burst and lysosomal enzymes, not adhesion molecules.

questions.q: Explain how the vascular and cellular changes of acute inflammation produce its classic signs.
markScheme: Arteriolar dilation (e.g. histamine, prostaglandins, nitric oxide) increases blood flow: redness and heat
Increased venular permeability lets protein-rich exudate into tissues: swelling
Mediators such as bradykinin and prostaglandins sensitise nerve endings: pain
Neutrophils are recruited by rolling, adhesion, transmigration and chemotaxis
Swelling and pain cause loss of function
questions.modelAnswer: Mediators such as histamine, prostaglandins and nitric oxide dilate arterioles, so more blood flows through the area, making it red and warm. Venules become leaky, so protein-rich fluid (exudate) escapes into the tissue and it swells. Bradykinin and prostaglandins sensitise pain nerve endings, and the swelling stretches tissue, causing pain. Meanwhile neutrophils roll on selectins, adhere through integrins and ICAM-1, migrate between endothelial cells and follow chemotactic signals such as IL-8 and C5a to the site. The combination of pain and swelling leads to loss of function.

questions.q: A virus-infected epithelial cell is killed by a cytotoxic T cell. Which molecule on the infected cell presented the viral peptide?
questions.why: Viral proteins made inside the cell are processed and shown on MHC class I, which almost all nucleated cells express, and this is what CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognise. MHC class II is the common mix-up: it presents peptides from engulfed material to CD4 helper T cells and is found on professional antigen-presenting cells, not ordinary epithelium. CD4 is a co-receptor on helper T cells, not a presenting molecule. CD28 is the co-stimulatory receptor on T cells.

questions.q: Blood tests show high levels of specific IgM, with little specific IgG, against a virus. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Immunity from a vaccine given in childhood
Infection years ago with lasting immunity
questions.why: IgM is made first in a primary response, so a high specific IgM with little IgG points to a recent first infection. Past infection with lasting immunity would show mainly IgG, because the IgM response fades and memory produces IgG. Maternal antibody that crosses the placenta is IgG, not IgM, so passive transfer cannot explain it. Childhood vaccination likewise leaves IgG and memory cells, not a high IgM years later.

questions.q: Describe how a T-dependent B-cell response produces high-affinity IgG antibodies.
markScheme: B cell binds antigen via its B-cell receptor, internalises it and presents peptide on MHC class II
Helper T cell (activated earlier by a dendritic cell) recognises the same antigen and provides help via CD40L–CD40 and cytokines
In the germinal centre, class switching changes IgM to IgG
Somatic hypermutation plus selection for best binding gives affinity maturation
B cells become plasma cells (secrete antibody) and memory B cells
questions.modelAnswer: A naive B cell binds antigen through its B-cell receptor, takes it in and displays peptides from it on MHC class II. A CD4 helper T cell that was activated by a dendritic cell presenting the same antigen recognises this complex and helps the B cell: CD40 ligand on the T cell binds CD40 on the B cell, and cytokines are released. Some activated B cells enter germinal centres in lymph nodes. There, class switching changes the antibody from IgM to IgG (or IgA or IgE) while keeping the same specificity, and somatic hypermutation alters the antigen-binding region; B cells with the best-binding receptors are selected to survive, so affinity rises. The selected cells become plasma cells that secrete high-affinity IgG, or long-lived memory B cells.

questions.q: Why are plain polysaccharide vaccines poorly effective in children under about two years old?
options: Maternal IgA in breast milk neutralises the vaccine
Infants lack MHC class I molecules
Polysaccharides are destroyed by stomach acid
Polysaccharides are T-independent antigens, and infants make weak T-independent antibody responses with little memory
questions.why: Polysaccharides cannot be presented to helper T cells, so they trigger only T-independent B-cell responses, which are weak in young children and produce little memory; conjugating them to protein fixes this. Breast-milk IgA protects the infant's gut and does not neutralise an injected vaccine. Infants do express MHC class I, and class I is not the issue for antibody responses to polysaccharide anyway. These vaccines are injected, not swallowed, so stomach acid is irrelevant.

questions.q: A woman develops an itchy rash where a nickel watch strap touched her skin, appearing about two days after contact. Which type of hypersensitivity is this?
questions.why: Contact dermatitis to nickel is delayed, T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity (type IV), typically appearing one to three days after exposure. Type I is IgE-mediated and appears within minutes, as in urticaria or anaphylaxis, so the two-day delay rules it out. Type II involves antibodies against cell-surface or tissue antigens, as in transfusion reactions. Type III involves immune complex deposition, as in serum sickness, not a skin reaction confined to the contact site.

questions.q: Compare live attenuated and inactivated vaccines, giving one example of each and one safety consideration.
markScheme: Live attenuated: weakened organism replicates, strong long-lasting antibody and T-cell response, often fewer doses (example: MMR or BCG)
Inactivated or subunit/toxoid: cannot replicate, weaker response, usually needs adjuvant and boosters (example: inactivated polio, tetanus toxoid)
Safety: live vaccines generally avoided in significant immunosuppression and in pregnancy
Inactivated vaccines cannot cause the infection and can be used in immunosuppressed people (though response may be weaker)
questions.modelAnswer: Live attenuated vaccines, such as MMR, contain weakened organisms that replicate briefly, mimicking natural infection; they give strong, long-lasting antibody and T-cell responses, often from fewer doses. Inactivated vaccines, such as inactivated polio vaccine, or toxoids such as tetanus, cannot replicate, so they give weaker responses and usually need adjuvants and booster doses. The key safety point is that live vaccines can cause disease in people with significant immunosuppression and are generally avoided in them and in pregnancy, whereas inactivated vaccines cannot cause the infection and can be given to immunosuppressed people, although their response may be weaker.

questions.q: A disease has R0 = 10. A vaccine is 95% effective. What is the herd immunity threshold (the proportion of the population that must be immune)?
questions.why: The threshold is 1 − 1/R0 = 1 − 1/10 = 0.9, so 90% must be immune; vaccine effectiveness does not change the threshold itself. 10% is 1/R0, the proportion that can stay susceptible, not the proportion that must be immune. 94.7% is 0.9 ÷ 0.95, which is the vaccine coverage needed to reach the threshold, answering a different question. 85.5% comes from multiplying 0.9 by 0.95 instead of dividing, which is wrong for both quantities.

questions.q: An infection has R0 = 4. In a town, 60% of people are immune. Using the simple model, what is the effective reproduction number?
questions.why: Effective R ≈ R0 × proportion susceptible = 4 × (1 − 0.6) = 4 × 0.4 = 1.6, so cases would still increase. 2.4 multiplies by the proportion immune (0.6) instead of the proportion susceptible. 3.4 subtracts 0.6 from R0, mixing a proportion with a count of cases. 6.7 divides R0 by 0.6, which would make immunity increase spread.

questions.q: A cluster of diarrhoea and vomiting follows a wedding meal. Outline how the outbreak would be investigated and controlled.
markScheme: Confirm the outbreak and diagnosis (clinical details, stool samples)
Write a case definition and find cases (guest list, questionnaires)
Plot an epidemic curve: a single sharp peak suggests a point source such as one meal
Compare food histories of ill and well guests to identify the likely vehicle
Control: remove the source, hygiene advice (soap and water for norovirus), exclude ill food handlers, notify/inform the health protection team
questions.modelAnswer: First confirm that there really is an outbreak and establish the likely diagnosis, collecting clinical details and stool samples. Write a case definition (who counts as a case, when and where), then actively find cases, for example by contacting everyone on the guest list. Plot an epidemic curve: a single sharp peak about one incubation period after the meal suggests a point source. Compare what ill and well guests ate to find the food most strongly associated with illness. Control measures are to withdraw the suspected food, investigate the kitchen, exclude ill food handlers until they are no longer infectious, give hygiene advice (soap and water, since alcohol rub is less reliable against norovirus) and work with the local UKHSA health protection team, notifying as required.

questions.q: A man newly diagnosed with HIV says he will not start treatment because he fears his workmates will find out. Which concept best explains the barrier he describes?
questions.why: He fears being labelled and discriminated against if his diagnosis becomes known, which is anticipated stigma, a well-recognised reason for delayed or refused HIV care. The sick role describes the rights and duties society gives a sick person; if anything it would push him to accept treatment. Antigenic drift is a viral mechanism of gradual mutation, unrelated to behaviour. The inverse care law is about good care being least available where it is most needed, a population pattern rather than this man's personal fear.

questions.q: Why might a patient in a single room under contact precautions for MRSA be at risk of poorer care, according to research on isolation?
options: Isolation rooms increase transmission of MRSA to the patient
Studies have linked isolation with fewer clinician contacts and more anxiety and depression
Isolated patients are legally barred from visitors
Contact precautions require stopping all antibiotics
questions.why: Reviews of mainly observational studies associate contact isolation with more anxiety and depression and, in some studies, fewer visits from clinicians, so staff should make deliberate efforts to check on isolated patients. Isolation aims to reduce MRSA transmission, not increase it. There is no legal ban on visitors; visitors are usually allowed with precautions. Contact precautions concern hand hygiene, gloves and aprons, and do not mean stopping antibiotics.

questions.q: A student is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. Describe four social or psychological effects this diagnosis might have on her.
markScheme: Stigma or fear of stigma (TB's history; fear of being seen as dirty or contagious)
Anxiety about infecting family or housemates, and the disruption of contact tracing
Social isolation during the infectious period (time off study or work, loneliness)
Financial or academic disruption, and burden of a long treatment course affecting mood and adherence
questions.modelAnswer: She may feel stigmatised, or fear that others will see her as dirty or dangerous because of TB's history, which can make her reluctant to tell friends. She may be anxious that she has infected housemates or family, and find contact tracing embarrassing. During the infectious period she may need to stay away from university, causing isolation and loneliness. The long treatment course can disrupt study, work and income, and the strain may cause low mood, which in turn can affect adherence. Addressing these openly and offering support helps her complete treatment.

questions.q: Broth tubes containing an antibiotic at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 8 mg/L are inoculated with a bacterium. After incubation, the 0.25, 0.5 and 1 mg/L tubes are cloudy and the others are clear. What is the MIC?
questions.why: The MIC is the lowest concentration with no visible growth: the first clear tube is 2 mg/L. 1 mg/L is the highest concentration that still allowed growth, a common off-by-one-tube slip. 8 mg/L is simply the highest concentration tested; it also inhibits growth but is not the minimum. 0.25 mg/L is the lowest concentration tested, and it did not inhibit growth.

questions.q: A Staphylococcus aureus isolate is resistant to flucloxacillin and other β-lactams because it carries the mecA gene. What does this gene do?
options: Encodes a β-lactamase that hydrolyses the drug
Encodes an efflux pump that removes the drug
Removes porins so the drug cannot enter
Encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with low affinity for β-lactams
questions.why: mecA encodes PBP2a, a transpeptidase that keeps building the cell wall because β-lactams bind it poorly; this target change is what defines MRSA. β-lactamase production is a different, common resistance mechanism in staphylococci, but flucloxacillin is designed to resist staphylococcal penicillinase, so it does not explain this pattern. Efflux pumps are important in other resistance but are not what mecA encodes. Porin loss limits entry through the Gram-negative outer membrane; S. aureus is Gram-positive and has no outer membrane porins.

questions.q: Using named drug classes, explain how antibacterial drugs achieve selective toxicity. (Do not give doses.)
markScheme: Principle: target present in bacteria but absent or different in humans
Cell wall: β-lactams block peptidoglycan cross-linking (humans have no peptidoglycan)
Ribosome: aminoglycosides/tetracyclines (30S) or macrolides (50S) target 70S bacterial ribosomes, not human 80S
Nucleic acid: fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV
Folate: sulfonamides and trimethoprim block bacterial folate synthesis; humans take in folate from diet
questions.modelAnswer: Selective toxicity means hitting a target that bacteria have and human cells lack, or that differs enough to be hit selectively. β-lactams such as penicillins block the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, which human cells do not have. Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines bind the 30S subunit and macrolides the 50S subunit of the bacterial 70S ribosome, sparing our 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes. Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Sulfonamides and trimethoprim block steps in folate synthesis; bacteria must make their own folate, whereas we absorb it from food, and trimethoprim binds bacterial dihydrofolate reductase far more strongly than the human enzyme.

questions.q: A previously healthy 30-year-old develops pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. Describe how the innate and adaptive immune systems respond to this infection, and explain why a conjugate vaccine protects infants against pneumococcal disease when a plain polysaccharide vaccine does not.
markScheme: Barriers breached; organism is a Gram-positive encapsulated coccus; capsule resists phagocytosis
Innate recognition by PRRs (e.g. TLRs) on alveolar macrophages; cytokines IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6; fever and CRP
Complement activation (alternative/lectin, later classical) with C3b opsonisation and C5a recruitment of neutrophils; neutrophil recruitment steps
Dendritic cells carry antigen to lymph nodes; CD4 T-cell activation (signals 1–3); Th17/neutrophil help
B-cell response: IgM then class-switched IgG via T-cell help; anti-capsule antibody opsonises, enabling phagocytosis; memory
Plain polysaccharide is T-independent: weak in under-twos, little memory
Conjugate links polysaccharide to protein: helper T cells recruited, class switching, affinity maturation and memory in infants
Clear structure, correct terminology, links between innate and adaptive arms
questions.modelAnswer:
Streptococcus pneumoniae is a Gram-positive coccus with a polysaccharide capsule. When it reaches the alveoli, the capsule is its main defence, because it hinders complement deposition and phagocytosis.

Innate response. Alveolar macrophages recognise pneumococcal components through pattern recognition receptors such as Toll-like receptors. They release IL-1, TNF-α and IL-6, which cause fever by raising the hypothalamic set point and, through IL-6, make the liver produce C-reactive protein, which can itself bind pneumococcal cell wall components and activate complement. Complement is activated by the alternative and lectin pathways, and later by the classical pathway once antibody appears. C3b coats the bacteria (opsonisation), and C5a attracts neutrophils. Endothelium in the lung becomes activated: neutrophils roll on selectins, adhere through integrins binding ICAM-1, migrate into the alveoli and follow chemotactic gradients. Leaky vessels and the influx of neutrophils fill the alveoli with exudate, producing consolidation. Neutrophils ingest opsonised bacteria and kill them using the respiratory burst and lysosomal enzymes.

Adaptive response. Dendritic cells take up bacterial antigens and migrate to lymph nodes, presenting peptides on MHC class II to naive CD4 T cells with co-stimulation (CD80/86 to CD28) and cytokines. Helper T cells, including Th17 cells that promote neutrophil recruitment, expand. B cells that recognise pneumococcal antigens make IgM first. With T-cell help through CD40 ligand and cytokines, B cells in germinal centres class-switch to IgG and undergo affinity maturation. Anti-capsular IgG is especially protective: it opsonises the bacteria through Fc receptors and activates complement, overcoming the capsule's defence. Memory B and T cells give faster protection on re-exposure to the same serotype.

Vaccines in infants. A plain polysaccharide vaccine is a T-independent antigen: polysaccharide cannot be processed and presented on MHC class II, so it activates B cells by cross-linking their receptors without T-cell help. Children under about two years make weak T-independent responses, and such responses produce little class switching or memory. A conjugate vaccine links capsular polysaccharide to a carrier protein. B cells specific for the polysaccharide take up the conjugate and present peptides from the carrier protein to helper T cells. This converts the response into a T-dependent one, giving class-switched, high-affinity IgG against the capsule and immunological memory, even in infants. This is why conjugate vaccines are used in the UK infant schedule.

questions.q: Antimicrobial resistance has been called a major threat to modern medicine. Explain how bacteria become resistant to antibiotics and how resistance spreads, and discuss how antimicrobial stewardship in the UK aims to limit it. (Do not give doses.)
markScheme: Distinguishes intrinsic vs acquired resistance
Acquisition by mutation and horizontal gene transfer (conjugation, transformation, transduction); plasmids may carry several resistance genes
Mechanisms with examples: enzymatic inactivation (β-lactamases, ESBLs, carbapenemases), altered target (mecA/PBP2a, VRE), reduced permeability (porins), efflux
Selection pressure: any antimicrobial use, especially broad-spectrum and unnecessary use; spread between people, in healthcare and via animals/environment (One Health)
Stewardship principles: right drug, right time, right duration; narrowest effective spectrum; cultures before treatment; review
UK specifics: NICE NG15; UKHSA Start smart then focus with 48–72 h review (cease, amend, refer, extend, switch); national action plan 2024–2029 targets
Infection prevention and vaccination reduce the need for antibiotics
Balanced discussion, e.g. tension between treating sepsis promptly and avoiding unnecessary broad-spectrum use
questions.modelAnswer:
Resistance can be intrinsic or acquired. Intrinsic resistance is a natural property of a species: vancomycin cannot cross the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, and aminoglycosides are not taken up by anaerobes. Acquired resistance arises when a previously susceptible organism changes.

Bacteria acquire resistance by mutation or by gaining genes from other bacteria. Because bacteria divide rapidly, rare mutations (for example in DNA gyrase, giving fluoroquinolone resistance) appear in large populations. Horizontal gene transfer is often more important: conjugation passes plasmids through a pilus, transformation takes up free DNA and transduction uses bacteriophages. Plasmids can carry several resistance genes together, so one transfer may confer multi-drug resistance.

The resistance genes act through a few mechanisms. Enzymes may destroy the drug: β-lactamases, extended-spectrum β-lactamases that inactivate many cephalosporins, and carbapenemases. The target may change: MRSA carries mecA, encoding PBP2a, which β-lactams bind poorly, and vancomycin-resistant enterococci alter the D-Ala-D-Ala target. Entry may be reduced by losing porins, or the drug may be pumped out by efflux pumps.

Resistance spreads because every use of an antimicrobial kills susceptible organisms and leaves resistant ones, including among normal flora. Broad-spectrum and unnecessary use, such as antibiotics for viral infections, adds selection pressure. Resistant organisms then spread between patients through hands and the environment in hospitals, in the community and between people, animals and the environment, which is why a One Health approach is advocated.

Stewardship aims to keep antimicrobials effective while still treating infection promptly. NICE guideline NG15 (2015) sets out organisational systems for it. UKHSA's Start smart then focus toolkit, updated in 2023, asks prescribers to start antibiotics only with evidence of infection, to take cultures first where possible without delaying treatment of sepsis, to follow local guidelines and to document the indication and a duration or review date. At 48 to 72 hours the prescription is reviewed and the decision recorded: cease, amend (usually to a narrower drug), refer to outpatient or virtual-ward care, extend with a stop date, or switch from intravenous to oral. The UK national action plan for 2024 to 2029 sets targets including a 5% reduction in total human antibiotic use from the 2019 to 2020 baseline by 2029 and 70% of use from the Access category of the UK-adapted AWaRe classification, the antibiotics with lower resistance potential.

Prevention also reduces demand for antibiotics: hand hygiene and other infection control, vaccination (for example against pneumococcus and influenza), and clean water and sanitation.

There are tensions. A septic patient needs prompt broad treatment, and withholding it costs lives, but continuing broad-spectrum drugs without review fuels resistance and C. difficile. Stewardship resolves this by treating promptly and then reviewing, rather than by withholding treatment.
